h: A power station with a past
p: The building has a story worth knowing before you go in. Bankside Power Station was designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott, the same architect behind Battersea Power Station and the classic red telephone box, and it generated electricity for London until 1981. Swiss architects Herzog and de Meuron then reimagined it as a gallery, and it opened to the public in 2000. Later, a twisting brick extension was added, giving the gallery much more room for installations, performance and big immersive works.

Down in the bowels of the building, the old oil tanks have been turned into raw, atmospheric spaces for performance, film and live art, so keep an eye out for what's happening there. Upstairs, the collection is arranged by theme rather than strictly by date, which makes it easier to compare how different artists tackled the same ideas, whether that's cities, the body or materials.

For a first visit, a couple of hours is plenty to get a good feel for the place without your brain turning to mush. Pick a floor, wander, then come back up for air. Families can usually find free activities and creative sessions on certain days, and the big spaces mean little ones can move around without feeling hemmed in.

Bankside has loads to pair with it. Walk east along the river past Shakespeare's Globe to reach Southwark Cathedral and the replica of Sir Francis Drake's Golden Hinde, tucked into a tiny dock. Borough Market is perfect for grazing on lunch, and if you fancy staying on the north side after crossing the Millennium Bridge, St Paul's is right there waiting.
